title: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents

topics.title: Continental drift: Wegener, Pangaea and Panthalassa

learn.hook: Look at a world map: the bulge of Brazil seems to fit into the curve of West Africa like jigsaw pieces. A weather scientist took that hint seriously.
points: Continents cover about 29% of the earth's surface; the rest is under oceans. The positions of continents and oceans have not always been the same.

Early ideas: Abraham Ortelius, a Dutch map maker, suggested as early as 1596 that the Americas, Europe and Africa were once joined. Antonio Pellegrini drew a map showing the three continents together.
Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist, gave a comprehensive argument in 1912: the continental drift theory.
Wegener said all continents formed one supercontinent, Pangaea ('all earth'), surrounded by one mega-ocean, Panthalassa ('all water').
Around 200 million years ago, Pangaea began to split, first into two large landmasses: Laurasia (northern) and Gondwanaland (southern). These later broke into today's continents.

example.q: Name the two landmasses Pangaea first split into and say which one India was part of.
steps: About 200 million years ago Pangaea split into two.
The northern part was Laurasia.
The southern part was Gondwanaland.
India lies with the southern landmasses (Africa, South America, Australia, Antarctica), so it was part of Gondwanaland.
example.answer: Laurasia (north) and Gondwanaland (south); India was in Gondwanaland.

learn.reallife: The Gondwana coalfields of the Damodar, Mahanadi and Godavari valleys get their name from Gondwanaland, the ancient southern supercontinent.

topics.title: Evidence for drift: jigsaw fit, rock ages and tillite

learn.hook: Ancient glacier deposits are found in hot India and Africa today. Ice never formed there in the present climate, so the land itself must have moved.
points: Jigsaw fit: the facing shorelines of Africa and South America match remarkably. In 1964 Bullard used a computer programme to find the best fit of the Atlantic margins; the fit was almost perfect at the 1,000-fathom line rather than the present shoreline.
Rocks of the same age across oceans: radiometric dating shows that a belt of ancient rocks, 2,000 million years old, on the Brazil coast matches rocks in western Africa.
The earliest marine deposits along the coasts of South America and Africa are of Jurassic age, suggesting that the ocean did not exist before that time.

Tillite is a sedimentary rock formed from glacial deposits. The Gondwana system of sediments of India has counterparts in six landmasses of the Southern Hemisphere (Africa, Falkland Islands, Madagascar, Antarctica and Australia, besides India).
Thick tillite at the base of the Gondwana system shows extensive, prolonged glaciation. It is clear evidence of past climates and of the drifting of continents.

example.q: Why was Bullard's 1964 fit done at the 1,000-fathom line and not at today's coastline?
steps: Present coastlines change with sea level, erosion and deposition.
The true edge of a continent is the continental margin, below sea level.
Matching at the 1,000-fathom depth line compares the real continental edges.
This gave an almost perfect fit.
example.answer: Because the 1,000-fathom line is closer to the true edge of the continents than the shifting shoreline.

learn.reallife: Talchir tillite in Odisha, part of India's Gondwana rocks, records an ice age when India lay much closer to the South Pole.

Answer: Extensive and prolonged glaciation

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Glacial tillite found in India supports the idea of continental drift.
Reason (R): Tillite is a rock formed by the cooling of volcanic lava.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true: thick tillite in the Gondwana rocks of tropical India shows India was once in a cold, glaciated region. R is false: tillite is a sedimentary rock formed from glacial deposits, not from lava.
steps: A: glacial tillite in India supports continental drift. True.
R: tillite forms from cooling volcanic lava. False; it forms from glacial deposits.
So A is true but R is false.
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Confuses tillite (glacial) with igneous rocks like basalt

topics.title: Evidence for drift: placers and fossils; Wegener's forces

learn.hook: Ghana's coast has rich gold deposits but no gold-bearing rock nearby. The 'source' lies across the Atlantic, in Brazil!
points: Placer deposits: rich placer gold deposits occur on the Ghana coast, but there are no source rocks there. The gold-bearing veins are in Brazil, so Ghana's gold must have come from the Brazil plateau when the two continents lay side by side.
Distribution of fossils: identical land or freshwater species on either side of marine barriers need an explanation.
Lemurs occur in India, Madagascar and Africa, which led some to imagine a connecting landmass called 'Lemuria'.
Mesosaurus, a small reptile of shallow brackish water, is found only in the southern Cape province of South Africa and the Iraver formations of Brazil, now 4,800 km apart with an ocean between them.

Force for drifting: Wegener suggested the pole-fleeing force (linked to the earth's rotation and its equatorial bulge) and the tidal force (due to the attraction of the moon and the sun). Most scholars considered these forces totally inadequate.

example.q: Why is Mesosaurus strong evidence for drift?
steps: Mesosaurus lived in shallow brackish water.
It could not have swum across a 4,800 km wide ocean.
Yet its fossils occur in both South Africa and Brazil.
So the two areas must once have been joined.
example.answer: A shallow-water reptile could not cross an ocean, so South Africa and Brazil must have been connected.

learn.reallife: Grey slender lorises of Sri Lanka and India belong to the same primate group as Madagascar's lemurs, part of the puzzle that once inspired the 'Lemuria' idea.

topics.title: Post-drift studies: convection currents and ocean floor mapping

learn.hook: Wegener's big gap was 'What pushes the continents?' Two decades later, Arthur Holmes suggested the answer: the mantle is slowly boiling.
points: Convectional current theory: in the 1930s Arthur Holmes discussed convection currents in the mantle, generated by radioactive elements causing thermal differences. He argued that a system of such currents exists throughout the mantle.
Mapping of the ocean floor in the post-Second World War period showed that the ocean floor is not a vast plain but full of relief.
It revealed submerged mountain ranges and deep trenches, mostly located closer to the continental margins. Mid-oceanic ridges were found to be the most active in volcanic eruptions.
Dating showed that the oceanic crust is much younger than the continental areas.
Rocks equidistant from the crest of a mid-oceanic ridge, on either side, are remarkably similar in their constituents and age.

example.q: How did ocean floor mapping help revive the idea of moving continents?
steps: It found mid-oceanic ridges with active volcanism, i.e. a place where new crust may form.
It found deep trenches near continents, i.e. a place where crust may sink.
Ocean crust turned out to be young, and rocks matched symmetrically about the ridge.
These suggested the ocean floor itself is moving, leading to sea floor spreading.
example.answer: By revealing active ridges, trenches, young ocean crust and symmetric rocks: signs of a moving ocean floor.

learn.reallife: India's National Institute of Oceanography in Goa and the research vessel Sagar Kanya have mapped parts of the Indian Ocean ridges using similar techniques.

learn.hook: The longest mountain chain on earth is not the Himalaya or the Andes. It is hidden under the oceans.
points: Based on depth and relief, the ocean floor is divided into three major divisions: continental margins, deep sea basins and mid-ocean ridges.
Continental margins form the transition between continental shores and deep-sea basins. They include the continental shelf, continental slope, continental rise and deep oceanic trenches.
Abyssal plains are extensive plains between the continental margins and mid-oceanic ridges. Continental sediments that move beyond the margins are deposited here.
Mid-oceanic ridges form an interconnected chain of mountains within the ocean: the longest mountain chain on the earth's surface, though submerged.
A mid-oceanic ridge has a central rift system at the crest, a fractionated plateau, and a flank zone along its length. The rift at the crest is a zone of intense volcanic activity.

example.q: A ship sails from the coast of Mumbai straight to the Carlsberg Ridge in the Arabian Sea. List the ocean-floor features it crosses in order.
steps: Near the coast: continental shelf.
Then the steep continental slope and the continental rise.
Then the deep, flat abyssal plain (deep sea basin).
Finally the mid-oceanic ridge (Carlsberg Ridge) with its central rift.
example.answer: Shelf → slope → rise → abyssal plain → mid-oceanic ridge.

learn.reallife: Mumbai High, India's biggest offshore oilfield, lies on the continental shelf, the shallow part of the continental margin.

learn.hook: Plot every earthquake and volcano on a world map and they are not scattered randomly. They draw lines, and those lines outline the plates.
points: A line of earthquake dots runs through the central Atlantic Ocean, almost parallel to the coastlines, and extends into the Indian Ocean. It coincides with the mid-oceanic ridges.
In the Indian Ocean the line branches a little south of the Indian subcontinent: one branch goes into East Africa and the other meets a line running from Myanmar to New Guinea.
A second belt of concentration coincides with the Alpine-Himalayan system and the rim of the Pacific Ocean.
Earthquake foci along mid-oceanic ridges are at shallow depths, while along the Alpine-Himalayan belt and the Pacific rim they are deep-seated.
Volcanoes show a similar pattern. The rim of the Pacific is called the 'rim of fire' (Ring of Fire) because of its many active volcanoes. Map work: locate the Ring of Fire and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

example.q: An earthquake has a shallow focus and lies in the middle of the Atlantic. Another has a deep focus near Japan. Explain the difference.
steps: The mid-Atlantic quake lies on the mid-oceanic ridge, where plates pull apart; foci there are shallow.
The Japan quake lies on the Pacific rim, where one plate sinks under another; foci there are deep-seated.
So the type of zone decides the focal depth.
example.answer: Ridges have shallow-focus quakes; the Pacific rim (and Alpine-Himalayan belt) has deep-seated quakes.

learn.reallife: India sits next to the Alpine-Himalayan belt, which is why the Himalayan states and the North-East fall in India's highest seismic zone.

learn.hook: The ocean floor is like a giant tape recorder: as new rock forms at the ridges, it 'records' the earth's magnetic field, which keeps flipping.
points: Palaeomagnetic studies show that rocks on either side of a mid-oceanic ridge form parallel stripes of normal and reverse magnetic polarity, matching on both sides.

Rocks equidistant from the crest are similar in age, chemical composition and magnetic properties. Rocks closest to the ridge have normal polarity and are the youngest; age increases with distance from the crest.
Ocean crust rocks are much younger than continental rocks: no oceanic crust is more than 200 million years old, while some continental rocks are as old as 3,200 million years.
Sediments on the ocean floor are unexpectedly thin. If the ocean floor were as old as the continents, much thicker sediments would have collected.
Deep trenches have deep-seated earthquakes, while mid-oceanic ridges have shallow-focus earthquakes.

example.q: Rock A lies 10 km from a ridge crest and rock B lies 200 km away on the same side. Which is older and why?
steps: New crust forms at the ridge crest and moves outwards.
Rocks nearer the crest formed more recently.
Rock A is nearer the crest, so it is younger.
Rock B, farther away, formed earlier and is older.
example.answer: Rock B is older, because age increases away from the ridge crest.

topics.title: Hess's sea floor spreading and the idea of plates

learn.hook: If new ocean floor forms at the ridges every year, the earth should be growing. It isn't. So where does old ocean floor go?
points: Harry Hess (1961) proposed sea floor spreading: constant eruptions at the crest of ridges rupture the oceanic crust; new lava wedges in and pushes the crust on either side, so the ocean floor spreads.

Because the spreading of one ocean does not shrink another and the ocean crust is young, Hess argued that the ocean floor pushed away from the ridge sinks at oceanic trenches and is consumed (subduction).
In the NCERT diagram, magma rises at the ridge, the floor moves away on both sides, and old floor sinks at a trench near a continent.
Plate tectonics was proposed in 1967 by McKenzie and Parker, and independently by Morgan.

A tectonic (lithospheric) plate is a massive, irregularly shaped slab of solid rock, generally made of both continental and oceanic lithosphere, moving horizontally over the asthenosphere as a rigid unit. The lithosphere is 5–100 km thick under oceans and about 200 km in continental areas.

example.q: Put Hess's model in order: crust sinks at trenches, magma erupts at the ridge, crust is pushed sideways.
steps: Magma erupts at the ridge crest and ruptures the crust.
New lava wedges in and pushes the crust to either side.
The floor moves away and finally sinks at an oceanic trench, where it is consumed.
example.answer: Eruption at ridge → crust pushed apart (spreading) → sinking and consumption at trench.

learn.reallife: The Andaman–Sumatra trench, where the Indian plate sinks below the Burma microplate, is the zone that produced the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.

learn.hook: The earth's surface is cracked into about seven giant pieces and many smaller ones, slowly jostling like rafts on a pond.
points: Seven major plates: Antarctica and the surrounding oceanic plate; North American plate; South American plate; Pacific plate; India-Australia-New Zealand plate; Africa with the eastern Atlantic floor plate; Eurasia and the adjacent oceanic plate.

Important minor plates: Cocos (between Central America and the Pacific plate), Nazca (between South America and the Pacific plate), Arabian (mostly the Saudi Arabian landmass), Philippine (between the Asiatic and Pacific plates), Caroline (between the Philippine and Indian plates, north of New Guinea) and Fuji (north-east of Australia).
A plate is called continental or oceanic depending on which occupies a larger part: the Pacific plate is largely oceanic; the Eurasian plate may be called continental.
It is the plate that moves, not the continent alone as Wegener believed. Continents are part of plates.
Palaeomagnetic data help reconstruct past positions of continents; the position of the Indian subcontinent (mostly Peninsular India) has been traced using rocks from the Nagpur area.

learn.hook: Plates can pull apart, crash together or grind sideways. Each kind of meeting builds a different landscape.
points: Divergent boundaries: new crust is generated as plates pull away from each other. These sites are called spreading sites. The best-known example is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the American plate(s) separate from the Eurasian and African plates.
Convergent boundaries: crust is destroyed as one plate dives under another. The place where a plate sinks is called a subduction zone.
Convergence can occur in three ways: between an oceanic and a continental plate; between two oceanic plates; and between two continental plates.
Transform boundaries: crust is neither produced nor destroyed; plates slide horizontally past each other.

Transform faults are planes of separation generally perpendicular to mid-oceanic ridges. They form because eruptions do not occur all along the crest at the same time, causing differential movement, and the earth's rotation also affects the separated blocks.

example.q: Classify each boundary: (a) Mid-Atlantic Ridge; (b) India pushing into Eurasia along the Himalaya; (c) plates sliding past each other along a fault crossing a ridge.
steps: (a) Plates pull apart, new crust forms → divergent.
(b) Two continental plates collide → convergent (continent–continent).
(c) Horizontal sliding, no crust made or destroyed → transform.

learn.reallife: The Himalaya are a continent–continent convergent boundary, while the Andaman trench is an ocean–continent type of convergence affecting India's islands.

quiz.explain: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the American plates separate from the Eurasian and African plates.
steps: The best-known divergent boundary is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
There the American plates separate from the Eurasian and African plates.
Answer: Mid-Atlantic Ridge
quiz.mistake: Picks a convergent example

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three types of convergence?
quiz.explain: Convergence occurs between ocean–continent, ocean–ocean and continent–continent plates.
steps: Convergence types: ocean–continent, ocean–ocean, continent–continent.
'Continental plate with asthenosphere' is not one of them.
Answer: Continental plate with asthenosphere
quiz.mistake: Invents a fourth type

quiz.q: Transform faults are generally oriented:
quiz.explain: Transform faults cut across ridges, roughly at right angles.
steps: Transform faults are planes of separation across ridges.
They are generally perpendicular to mid-oceanic ridges.
Answer: Perpendicular to mid-oceanic ridges
quiz.mistake: Thinks they run along the ridge

quiz.q: The collision of the Indian plate with the Eurasian plate is an example of:
quiz.explain: Both are continental plates meeting along the Himalaya.
steps: The Indian and Eurasian plates are both continental.
Their collision is continent–continent convergence.
Answer: Continent–continent convergence
quiz.mistake: Thinks India is an oceanic plate

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Transform faults develop across mid-oceanic ridges.
Reason (R): Eruptions do not occur all along the crest at the same time, causing differential movement of plate portions.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Unequal spreading along the crest, plus the earth's rotation, offsets ridge segments along transform faults.
steps: A: transform faults develop across mid-oceanic ridges. True.
R: eruptions don't occur all along the crest at once, causing differential movement. True.
Unequal spreading offsets ridge segments along faults, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks spreading is uniform along the ridge

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What happens where two plates meet?'
teach.praise: Divergent creates, convergent destroys, transform slides. Gappu has the plate-boundary trio!
teach.nudge: Describe the three types of plate boundaries and what happens to the crust in each.

revise.summary: Plates meet at divergent boundaries (crust created, e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge), convergent boundaries (crust destroyed in subduction zones) and transform boundaries (plates slide past; no crust made or destroyed).
focus: Identify the boundary type from an example
remember: Divergent = spreading site, new crust (Mid-Atlantic Ridge)
Convergent = subduction zone; ocean–continent, ocean–ocean, continent–continent
Transform = horizontal sliding; faults perpendicular to ridges
traps: Crust is not created at convergent boundaries
Transform faults are perpendicular, not parallel, to ridges

topics.title: Rates and forces of plate movement; drift vs plate tectonics

learn.hook: Plates move at roughly the speed your fingernails grow, yet over millions of years that adds up to whole oceans.
points: The strips of normal and reverse magnetic field parallel to mid-oceanic ridges help scientists determine the rates of plate movement.
Rates vary a lot: the Arctic Ridge is slowest (less than 2.5 cm/yr); the East Pacific Rise near Easter Island, in the South Pacific about 3,400 km west of Chile, is fastest (more than 15 cm/yr).

Force: the mantle is slowly convecting. Heated material rises, spreads, cools and sinks back, forming convection cells. The heat comes from radioactive decay and residual heat. Holmes first considered this in the 1930s, and it influenced Hess's ideas.

Continental drift (Wegener): continents move, driven by pole-fleeing and tidal forces. Plate tectonics: lithospheric plates, carrying both continents and ocean floor, move over the asthenosphere, driven by mantle convection.

example.q: A plate moves at 5 cm per year. How far does it move in 1 million years, in km?

learn.reallife: GPS stations of the Survey of India show the Indian plate moving north-east by a few centimetres every year.

items.q: 2 cm/yr for 100 years: distance in cm?
15 cm/yr for 10 years: distance in cm?
5 cm/yr for 1 million years: distance in km?
Fastest (15) minus slowest (2.5) rate, in cm/yr?

quiz.q: Which ridge has the slowest rate of plate movement?
quiz.explain: The Arctic Ridge moves at less than 2.5 cm/yr.
steps: The Arctic Ridge has the slowest rate.
It moves at less than 2.5 cm/yr.
Answer: Arctic Ridge
quiz.mistake: Picks the fastest ridge

quiz.q: The fastest rate of plate movement (more than 15 cm/yr) is found at the:
options: East Pacific Rise near Easter Island
quiz.explain: The East Pacific Rise near Easter Island spreads at over 15 cm/yr.
steps: The fastest rate, over 15 cm/yr, is at the East Pacific Rise.
It lies near Easter Island in the South Pacific.
Answer: East Pacific Rise near Easter Island
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Atlantic spreads fastest

quiz.q: What helps scientists determine the rates of plate movement?
options: Strips of normal and reverse magnetic field parallel to ridges
quiz.explain: Magnetic stripes of known age at known distances give spreading rates.
steps: Magnetic stripes parallel to ridges have known ages.
Their distances from the crest give spreading rates.
Answer: Strips of normal and reverse magnetic field parallel to ridges
quiz.mistake: Uses an unrelated feature

quiz.q: The two main sources of heat that drive mantle convection are:
options: Friction of winds and ocean currents
quiz.explain: Heat within the earth comes from radioactive decay and residual (primordial) heat.
steps: Mantle convection is driven by internal heat.
This heat comes from radioactive decay and residual heat.
Answer: Radioactive decay and residual heat
quiz.mistake: Uses external sources of heat

quiz.q: A plate moves 3 cm every year. How far will it move in 1,000 years? (Answer in metres.)
steps: Distance = 3 × 1,000 = 3,000 cm
Answer: 30 m
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert centimetres to metres

quiz.q: The main difference between continental drift and plate tectonics is that in plate tectonics:
options: Continents do not move at all
Plates carrying continents and ocean floor move, not continents alone
quiz.explain: Plate tectonics says the whole lithospheric plate moves.
steps: Drift: continents move alone.
Plate tectonics: whole plates with continents and ocean floor move.
Answer: Plates carrying continents and ocean floor move, not continents alone
quiz.mistake: Thinks plate tectonics denies movement

quiz.q: In a convection cell in the mantle, heated material:
options: Rises, spreads, cools and sinks back
quiz.explain: Hot material rises, spreads out, cools and sinks, repeating the cycle.
steps: In a convection cell, heated material rises and spreads.
Then it cools and sinks back, repeating the cycle.
Answer: Rises, spreads, cools and sinks back
quiz.mistake: Reverses the cycle

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Holmes's convection idea influenced Hess's thinking about sea floor spreading.
Reason (R): Convection in the mantle provides a force that can move the ocean floor away from ridges.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Rising convection currents beneath ridges offered a mechanism for spreading.
steps: A: Holmes's convection idea influenced Hess. True.
R: mantle convection provides a force to move the ocean floor away from ridges. True.
That force is the link Hess used, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two ideas are unrelated

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How fast do plates move, and what moves them?'
teach.praise: Slow Arctic Ridge, speedy East Pacific Rise, and mantle convection doing the pushing. Gappu is moving with the plates!
teach.nudge: Tell Gappu the slowest and fastest rates, and what force drives the plates.

revise.summary: Magnetic stripes give plate-movement rates, from under 2.5 cm/yr (Arctic Ridge) to over 15 cm/yr (East Pacific Rise). Mantle convection, powered by radioactive decay and residual heat, drives the plates.
remember: Arctic Ridge < 2.5 cm/yr; East Pacific Rise > 15 cm/yr
Convection cell: rise → spread → cool → sink
Heat sources: radioactive decay + residual heat
traps: The East Pacific Rise, not the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, is fastest
In plate tectonics continents do not move alone

learn.hook: India was once an island near Australia. It then raced north across an ocean and crashed into Asia, and the Himalaya are the wreckage.
points: The Indian plate includes Peninsular India and the Australian continental portions.

Boundaries: the northern boundary is a continent–continent convergence along the Himalaya. In the east it extends through the Rakinyoma Mountains of Myanmar towards the island arc along the Java Trench. The western margin follows the Kirthar Mountains of Pakistan and extends along the Makrana coast.

India was a large island off the Australian coast, separated from Asia by the Tethys Sea till about 225 million years ago. It began its northward journey about 200 million years ago, when Pangaea broke.

About 140 million years ago, the subcontinent lay as far south as 50°S. The outpouring of lava that formed the Deccan Traps began about 60 million years ago, while India was still close to the equator.
India collided with Asia about 40–50 million years ago, causing rapid uplift of the Himalaya. The process continues and the Himalaya are still rising.

example.q: Arrange in time order: Deccan Traps begin, India near 50°S, collision with Asia, start of the northward journey.
steps: Start of the northward journey: about 200 million years ago.
India near 50°S: about 140 million years ago.
Deccan Traps begin: about 60 million years ago.
Collision with Asia: about 40–50 million years ago.
example.answer: Northward journey (200 Ma) → near 50°S (140 Ma) → Deccan Traps (60 Ma) → collision (40–50 Ma).

learn.reallife: Marine fossils found high in the Himalaya, near Spiti and in Ladakh, are leftovers of the Tethys Sea floor lifted up by India's collision.

quiz.q: The Indian plate includes:
options: Peninsular India and the Australian continental portions
quiz.explain: The plate carries Peninsular India and the Australian continental portions.
steps: The Indian plate carries Peninsular India.
It also carries the Australian continental portions.
Answer: Peninsular India and the Australian continental portions
quiz.mistake: Thinks the plate covers only India

quiz.q: The northern boundary of the Indian plate is marked by:
options: A transform fault in the Arabian Sea
quiz.explain: The Indian and Eurasian continental plates meet along the Himalaya.

Both are continental: continent–continent convergence along the Himalaya.
Answer: Continent–continent convergence along the Himalaya
quiz.mistake: Picks a divergent feature

quiz.q: The western margin of the Indian plate follows the:
quiz.explain: The western margin follows the Kirthar Mountains and extends along the Makrana coast.
steps: The western margin follows the Kirthar Mountains of Pakistan.
It extends along the Makrana coast; the Rakinyoma Mountains are in the east.
Answer: Kirthar Mountains of Pakistan

quiz.q: Till about 225 million years ago, India was separated from Asia by the:
quiz.explain: The Tethys Sea lay between India and Asia.
steps: Till about 225 million years ago India was an island off Australia.
It was separated from Asia by the Tethys Sea.
Answer: Tethys Sea
quiz.mistake: Uses a modern sea name

quiz.q: About 140 million years ago, the Indian subcontinent was located as far south as:
quiz.explain: NCERT places it at about 50°S latitude then.
steps: About 140 million years ago the subcontinent lay far south.
Its position was about 50°S.
Answer: 50°S

quiz.q: The Deccan Traps formed around 60 million years ago when India was:
quiz.explain: The lava outpouring began about 60 million years ago with India still close to the equator.
steps: The Deccan Traps lava began about 60 million years ago.
India was then still close to the equator.
Answer: Close to the equator
quiz.mistake: Places India at its present latitude

quiz.q: India began its northward journey about 200 million years ago and collided with Asia about 50 million years ago. How long did the journey take, in million years?
quiz.explain: 200 − 50 = 150 million years.
steps: Start = 200 million years ago
Collision = 50 million years ago
Duration = 200 − 50 = 150 million years
Answer: 150
quiz.mistake: Adds the two figures

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The height of the Himalaya is still increasing.
Reason (R): The Indian plate continues to push against the Eurasian plate.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Continued convergence keeps uplifting the Himalaya.
steps: A: the Himalaya are still rising. True.
R: the Indian plate keeps pushing against the Eurasian plate. True.
Continued convergence keeps uplifting them, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the collision has stopped

teach.nudge: Tell Gappu where India started, when it moved, and how the Himalaya formed.

revise.summary: The Indian plate carries Peninsular India and Australia. Separated from Asia by the Tethys Sea, India moved north from about 200 million years ago, was near 50°S 140 million years ago, erupted the Deccan Traps 60 million years ago and hit Asia 40–50 million years ago.
remember: North: Himalaya (continent–continent); east: Rakinyoma Mts to Java Trench; west: Kirthar Mts, Makrana coast
